content: Adamantane, also known as tricyclodecane, is a colorless crystalline compound that emits an odor reminiscent of camphor. Its molecular formula is C10H16, classifying it as a cycloalkane and the simplest member of the diamondoid family. The compound was first identified in petroleum in 1933. Its name is derived from the Greek word adamantinos, which refers to steel or diamond, reflecting its diamond-like molecular structure. Among the isomers of C10H16, adamantane is the most thermodynamically stable. Adamantane was first synthesized in 1941 by Prelog. In 1957, Schleyer developed a more practical synthesis method, which involved hydrogenation of dicyclopentadiene followed by an acid-catalyzed skeletal rearrangement. Adamantane itself has limited applications due to its nature as an unfunctionalized hydrocarbon. It is used in certain dry etching masks and polymer formulations. In solid-state nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy, adamantane serves as a standard for chemical shift referencing. In dye lasers, it is employed to extend the lifespan of the gain medium, as it cannot undergo photoionization under atmospheric conditions due to its absorption bands being located in the vacuum-ultraviolet region of the spectrum. Recent studies have determined the photoionization energies of adamantane and larger diamondoid molecules. Condensed adamantanes, or diamondoids, have been isolated from petroleum fractions, where they are present in trace amounts. These compounds are of interest as molecular approximations of the cubic diamond framework, terminated with C-H bonds. A notable derivative, 1,3-dehydroadamantane, belongs to the propellane family. The 1-adamantyl group is a bulky substituent in organic and organometallic chemistry, valued for its stability, steric properties, and conformational rigidity. Some of the earliest persistent carbenes featured adamantyl substituents. Many molecules adopt cage-like structures resembling adamantane. Notable examples of compounds with adamantanoid motifs include P4O6, As4O6, P4O10 (also written as (PO)4O6), P4S10 (also written as (PS)4S6), and N4(CH2)6.
